fields.h1: Build a Telemedicine Consent Form for Video and Phone Visits
fields.hero_description: Get a telemedicine consent form that saves each patient's e-signature or spoken yes, plus a callback number for every visit.
fields.features_heading: Consent That Follows the Patient Into the Visit
fields.features_subheading: Every answer saves to a database you own, and the app can email the front desk when tomorrow's patient has not agreed yet.
fields.feature_1:
A link that goes out with the booking

The consent link rides along with the appointment confirmation. AHRQ advises sending the form in advance so patients can review it ahead of time, then e-sign on a phone.
fields.feature_2:
A verbal yes, with the staff member's name

Some patients never open a link. Staff mark Verbal consent given at check-in, and the app stamps the record with the staff member's name and the exact minute it happened.
fields.feature_3:
Everyone on the call, listed and approved

A caregiver, an interpreter, or a student clinician gets a line of their own. The patient approves each name before the visit starts, and the record keeps who was there.
fields.feature_4:
Where the patient is today

HHS advises confirming the patient's exact location at the beginning of each telemedicine appointment. Check-in asks for the full street address and saves it with that day's visit.
fields.feature_5:
Video, phone, or either

Patients pick the visit types they accept right on the form. The choice is saved next to their consent, so the scheduling screen can read it before anyone books a slot.
fields.feature_6:
A teach-back checklist for staff

AHRQ recommends teach-back to confirm patients understand. Staff get a short list of topics with a yes or no beside each: did the patient explain it in their own words?

fields.usecase_heading: What Happens Before the Doctor Joins
fields.tab_content_1:
When the patient has no portal, Noor reads it aloud

Desmond Achterberg has no portal login at Harlow Bend Family Practice. At 9:04 AM, medical assistant Noor Abernethy reads him the consent summary over video and he agrees out loud. She ticks Verbal consent given, and her name and the time save to his record before Dr. Sabine Oyelaran joins.
fields.tab_content_2:
Arturo said yes before Lucia joined the call

Sorrel Creek Geriatrics adds a line to check-in for anyone else on the call. Lucia Ferreira is joining her father Arturo's video visit, so the screen lists her as a participant, and Arturo's yes to having her there saves before the doctor starts.
fields.tab_content_3:
A frozen video at 3:22, with a callback number on file

Every session at Wrenfield Counseling opens with two questions for the client: the street address they are at right now, and a number to call back. When Tobias Lindqvist's video freezes at 3:22 PM, therapist Mireille Okonjo calls him on that number and finishes the session by phone.
fields.tab_content_4:
For Harriet, a phone slot instead of video

Harriet Kowalczyk ticked phone visits only on her consent at Thistledown Health. When Gideon Mbatha at the front desk tries to book her follow-up as a video visit, the scheduling screen blocks it and offers a phone slot at 2:30 PM Thursday instead.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Telemedicine Consent Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to create a telemedicine consent form that records each patient's agreement and the details staff need at check-in.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Type the consent you already use
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Hand the draft to your legal team
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Pick the ways a patient can agree
fields.howto_step_1_des: List what your current consent covers: what a video visit is, what happens if the call drops, who can see the record. Each item becomes one short section a patient can read on a phone.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Have your own counsel approve the wording before the first patient sees it. HHS notes that specific informed consent laws vary by state. The text is their call, not the form's.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Choose an e-signature on the link, a spoken yes at check-in, or both. AHRQ notes that in addition to verbal consent, a signature can be obtained through your patient portal and the U.S. mail.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Ask the visit types a patient accepts once, on the consent itself. Ask who else is on the call at every check-in, since a caregiver may join one visit and skip the next.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Put the sections, the ways to agree, and the check-in questions into one prompt. Emergent builds the telemedicine consent form and the database behind it. Change any of it later by prompting.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Give staff a list of today's visits
fields.howto_step_6_des: Ask for a staff view of today's video visits with a consent status beside each name: signed, verbal, or missing. The medical assistant works down that list before the clinician logs in.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Run a mock visit and drop the call
fields.howto_step_7_des: Book a test visit for a colleague, agree out loud, then end the video halfway through. Check that the record shows the verbal consent, the staff name, and a callback number.

faq_plan.q: What is a telemedicine consent form?
faq_plan.a: A telemedicine consent form records a patient's agreement to be seen by video or phone, after someone has explained what that involves. AHRQ says the purpose of consent forms is to document that a discussion took place and that the patient was informed and was able to understand the information provided.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a telemedicine consent form?
faq_plan.a: Write down what your current consent covers, have your counsel approve the wording, and then describe the form in one prompt to Emergent's AI form builder. Emergent builds the form, the staff check-in screen, and the database behind them from that prompt, and you change any of it by prompting. The free tier covers building and publishing.

faq_plan.q: How do I adapt a telemedicine consent form template to my practice?
faq_plan.a: Replace the template's visit types, video platform, and phone numbers with your own, then add a section for anything it skips, such as a caregiver on the call. AHRQ says of its own sample that it must be adapted before using it. If your telemedicine consent form template is a PDF, break each clause into its own screen. Have your counsel read the result before any patient signs.

faq_plan.q: How do I send a telemedicine consent form to a referred patient before the first visit?
faq_plan.a: Send the consent link the day the first visit is booked, not the morning of it. Once the referral form from the other practice is accepted and the visit is on the calendar, the app Emergent builds can email the patient the link. It can also send a reminder if the form is still unsigned two days before the visit.

faq_plan.q: When should a patient complete a telemedicine consent form?
faq_plan.a: Before the first telehealth visit, or at the very start of it. AHRQ notes that patients can give their consent verbally at the beginning of their first telehealth visit, and clinicians can document it in the medical record. Ask your counsel whether later visits need a fresh consent where you practice.

faq_plan.q: Can staff read a telemedicine consent form aloud to the patient?
faq_plan.a: Yes, and AHRQ suggests offering it to everyone: its guidance says to offer to read the form aloud to all patients. That includes the patient who opened the link and skimmed it. Keep one plain-language summary on the staff screen, and every staff member reads the same words in the same order.

faq_plan.q: Can a telemedicine consent form ask whether the visit may be recorded?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Put recording in its own yes-or-no question, apart from the main agreement. A patient can then accept the visit and still decline the recording, the same way a permanent makeup consent form keeps the photo checkbox separate. Whether and how your practice may record a visit is a question for your counsel.

faq_plan.q: What happens if a patient declines the telemedicine consent form?
faq_plan.a: Note the decline in the patient's record and offer another way to be seen, such as an in-person appointment. AHRQ's instruction on this is one line: if patients do not consent, note it in their medical records. Save the decline as its own answer with the date and the staff member's name, and check it before sending that patient another link.

faq_plan.q: How do I use teach-back with a telemedicine consent form?
faq_plan.a: Ask the patient to explain each section in their own words, one section at a time. AHRQ advises that you chunk out information into small segments and have your patient teach it back. If a patient repeats your words or reads the form back, explain that section a different way and ask again.

faq_plan.q: Where do signed telemedicine consent forms go after the patient submits?
faq_plan.a: Each signed form saves as a record in a database your practice owns, with the e-signature, the time it was given, and every answer on the form. The app can also send a copy to any tool with an API, such as your scheduling system. Emergent builds a waxing consent form with the same kind of table behind it.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is nine clinic PDFs: a page of I-understand clauses and one signature line, signed once and filed. None of them handles what happens around a video visit: a patient with no portal who agrees out loud, a family member who joins the call, a video that freezes mid-session, or a patient who agreed to phone visits only. This page builds those moments into the form, using only what HHS and AHRQ publish about telehealth consent (with their limits: rules vary by state, wording goes to the practice's legal team) and never says the form makes consent valid.
